1.explanation: By a stated future deadline (“by lunch”), the future perfect “will have finished” is the natural choice.

2.q: Where ______, had we not met her?
2.explanation: The final key marks D, but “had we not met her” is a past unreal condition and standard grammar would use “would she have stayed”; that exact form is not offered. The printed item/key conflict, so this question is held out from scoring pending clarification.

3.q: The cheese looks as if the rats __________ it.
3.explanation: The present perfect “have nibbled” describes the apparent completed action and its present result.

4.explanation: “All along” describes an action continuing over a period up to now, so the present perfect continuous fits.

5.q: The truck hit her while she __________ the road.
5.explanation: The past continuous marks the action in progress when the truck hit her.

6.q: I wish he __________ me that he was quitting.
6.explanation: “I wish” expresses regret about an earlier omission, so the past perfect “had told” is used.

7.q: Thank you so much for the bag. I __________ one for a long time.
7.explanation: The past perfect continuous describes the wish continuing before the bag was received.

8.q: Rakesh __________ for the competition these days.
8.explanation: “These days” points to a current temporary activity, so the present continuous fits.

9.q: That man __________ at the bus stop for the last hour.
9.explanation: “For the last hour” describes an action continuing until now, so the present perfect continuous fits.

10.q: Shall I tell that person that the last bus __________?
10.explanation: The present perfect “has gone” describes the bus leaving with a present result: it is no longer available.

11.explanation: To cast a slur on someone is to insult or damage their reputation; “bringing into disrepute” matches.

12.explanation: “Feet of clay” refers to a person’s hidden weakness or flaw, so C is the closest meaning.

13.explanation: A broken reed is an unreliable source of support.

opts.c: an achievement to be proud of

14.explanation: A “bee in one’s bonnet” is a persistent preoccupation or obsession.

opts.c: to do a thing in vain

15.explanation: The idiom means to keep pursuing or discussing something with no chance of success.

16.explanation: A “wet blanket” is someone or something that dampens others’ enjoyment.

17.explanation: “All agog” means very eager or excited.

18.explanation: To “turn tail” is to flee, especially out of fear.

19.explanation: “Red tapism” means excessive official procedures and resulting bureaucratic delay.

20.explanation: “Ever and anon” means occasionally or from time to time.

21.q: He wants someone to take photographs.

opts.a: Someone is wanted to take photographs
opts.b: He wants to be taking photographs
opts.c: He wants photographs to be taken

21.explanation: The passive infinitive “photographs to be taken” preserves the meaning that he wants others to take them.

22.q: He decided that the house should be sold.

opts.a: He decided the house to be sold
opts.b: He decided to sell the house
opts.c: He has decided to sell the house
opts.d: The house was decided to be sold by him

22.explanation: “He decided to sell the house” preserves the original decision and its subject.

23.q: I remember them taking me to the zoo.

opts.a: I remember I am being taken to the zoo
opts.b: They are taking me to the zoo
opts.c: I remember being taken to the zoo
opts.d: I remember that I was taken to the zoo by them

23.explanation: The final key marks B, but B removes “I remember” and changes the statement into a present action. C is the passive equivalent. Because the printed key conflicts with meaning-preserving grammar, this question is held out from scoring pending clarification.

24.q: Byron is said to have lived on vinegar and potatoes.

opts.a: They say that Byron lived on vinegar and potatoes
opts.b: Byron lived on vinegar and potatoes is said by them
opts.c: Vinegar and potatoes are lived on by Byron
opts.d: People said that Byron was living on vinegar and potatoes

24.explanation: The passive report “is said to have lived” changes to the impersonal active report “They say that Byron lived…”

25.q: He expected us to offer him the job.

opts.a: To offer him the job by us was expected by him
opts.b: The job was expected to be offered by us
opts.c: He expects the job to offer by us
opts.d: He expected to be offered the job

25.explanation: The passive infinitive “to be offered” keeps the job as the thing he expected to receive.

26.q: Rajendra Prasad was one of the greatest Indian leaders. (Comparative)

opts.a: Rajendra Prasad was as great as other Indian leaders.
opts.b: Rajendra Prasad was not the weakest of Indian leaders.
opts.c: Rajendra Prasad was greater than most other Indian leaders.
opts.d: Rajendra Prasad was also as great as other Indian leaders.

26.explanation: “One of the greatest” becomes “greater than most” in the comparative degree.

opts.b: Who does not like to be praised?
opts.c: Do everyone like to be praised?
opts.d: Doesn’t everybody likes to be praised?

27.explanation: The rhetorical question “Who does not like to be praised?” preserves the general assertion.

28.q: I wish I were a queen. (Exclamatory)

opts.a: Alas! if I were a queen!
opts.b: Oh! to have been a queen!
opts.d: Alas! I want to be queen!

28.explanation: “Oh, to be a queen!” expresses the same wish exclamatorily.

29.explanation: “It is not always easy” conveys that difficulty occurs often without changing the statement to an absolute.

30.q: What though the field be lost? (Assertive)

opts.a: The field will be lost eventually
opts.b: We are going to lose the field
opts.d: It does not matter even if the field is lost

30.explanation: The rhetorical question means that losing the field would not matter.

31.q: She was asked not to loiter in the gallery. (Affirmative)

opts.a: She was forbidden to loiter in the gallery
opts.b: She was told that she could not loiter in the gallery
opts.c: They asked her not to loiter in the gallery
opts.d: They forbade her to loiter in the gallery

31.explanation: “She was forbidden to loiter” states the same prohibition affirmatively.

32.q: It is better to lend than borrow. (Positive)

opts.a: To lend is better than to borrow
opts.b: Borrowing is not as good as lending
opts.c: To borrow is not better than lending

32.explanation: The positive-degree comparison uses “not as good as”: borrowing is not as good as lending.

33.q: His father is the most honest of all. (Comparative)

opts.a: No one else is so honest as his father
opts.b: None is more honest than his father
opts.c: His father is more honest than anybody else
opts.d: His father is as honest as anybody else

33.explanation: The final key marks C, but A, B and C all express the same comparison here. Multiple options are defensible, so the question is held out from scoring pending clarification.
33.reviewNote: The official key marks C, but A, B and C are grammatically valid comparative forms; held out from scoring pending clarification.

34.q: I wonder who is waiting __________ the table next to ours.
34.explanation: “Wait on a table” means to serve the people seated there; “on” is the required preposition.

35.q: Those are actions __________ which you should be ashamed.

36.explanation: “Lifted onto the table” describes movement to a position on top of it.

37.explanation: The final key marks C (“with”), but the standard collocation is “tenacious of life,” which is option B. This key/item conflict is held out from scoring pending clarification.
37.reviewNote: The official key marks C, but the standard phrase is “tenacious of life” (B); held out from scoring pending clarification.

38.q: The bee came in __________ the door.
38.explanation: “Through the door” describes entering via the doorway.

39.q: It is dangerous to enter __________ the enemy’s camp.
39.explanation: “Enter into” is the construction expected by the printed options for movement into a place.

40.q: Minority aspirations cannot forever be kept in check __________ the gun.
40.explanation: The phrase “with the gun” indicates the means used to keep aspirations in check.

41.q: A good judge never gropes __________ the conclusion.
41.explanation: “Grope for” means to search uncertainly for something, including a conclusion.

42.q: Under this heavy load the bridge will give __________.
42.explanation: “Give way” means to collapse or yield under pressure.

43.q: They quarrelled with me __________ the division of the booty.
43.explanation: “Quarrel about” introduces the subject of a disagreement.

44.q: It is more of self-interest than service. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined words “self-interest”.)
44.explanation: “Self-interest” names a motive or concern, so it is a noun.

45.q: All spoke in his favour. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “All”.)
45.explanation: “All” stands in for all the people who spoke, so it is a pronoun.

46.q: As he was poor, I helped him. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “As”.)
46.explanation: “As” joins the reason clause to the main clause, so it is a conjunction.

47.q: I’m just coming. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “just”.)
47.explanation: “Just” modifies “coming” by indicating that the action is happening now/very soon, so it functions as an adverb.

48.q: This is the road by which he came. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “which”.)
48.explanation: “Which” is a relative pronoun introducing the clause “by which he came.”

49.q: Every member is present. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “Every”.)
49.explanation: In traditional school grammar, “every” is a distributive adjective modifying “member.”

50.q: He showed much patience. (Identify the part of speech of the underlined word “much”.)
50.explanation: “Much” modifies the noun “patience,” so it is an adjective of quantity in traditional grammar.

51.q: He said to her, “What a cold day!”

opts.a: He told her that it was a cold day.
opts.b: He exclaimed that it was a cold day.
opts.c: He exclaimed sorrowfully that it was a cold day.
opts.d: He exclaimed that it was a very cold day.

51.explanation: An exclamation of “What a cold day!” is reported with “exclaimed” and the intensifier “very.”

52.q: The father warned his son that he should be aware of him.

opts.a: The father warned his son, “Be aware of him!”
opts.b: The father warned his son, “Be careful of him.”
opts.c: The father warns his son, “Beware of him.”
opts.d: The father warns, “Son, be aware of him.”

52.explanation: The reported warning “should be aware” returns to the direct imperative “Be aware.”

53.q: Harish said to me, “Why didn’t you come with us?”

opts.a: Harish asked me why I did not come with them.
opts.b: Harish asked me why didn’t I go with them.
opts.c: Harish asked me why I did not go with them.
opts.d: Harish asked whether I want to go with them.

53.explanation: In reported questions, use statement word order and backshift “you/us” to “I/them.”

opts.a: She said when she was a child she wasn’t afraid of ghosts.
opts.b: She told me that when she was a child she never feared ghosts.
opts.c: She said that when she was a child she wasn’t afraid of ghosts.
opts.d: She said that when she had been a child she wasn’t afraid of ghosts.

54.explanation: Option C reports the statement with the correct subject changes and preserves the past-time clause.

opts.a: He warned her to shoot if she didn’t keep quiet calmly.
opts.b: He said calmly that he shall shoot her if she doesn’t keep quiet.
opts.c: He warned her calmly that he would shoot her if she didn’t keep quiet.
opts.d: He warned with a calm voice that he should shoot if she is not quiet.

61.q:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Select the option that gives their correct order.
A. Therefore, I bought a good house in a respectable neighbourhood.
B. This made me eager to welcome the first guest at home and show my hospitality.
C. I intended to be a model citizen in the neighbourhood.
D. I decided it was time for me to settle down.
61.explanation: The sequence is D–A–C–B: deciding to settle down leads to buying a house, then the intention to be a model neighbour, which motivates welcoming a first guest.

62.q: Four sentences are given: A. I sow a seed. B. I saw the sapling. C. I saw the sprout. D. I saw the plant. Select the correct order.
62.explanation: The natural growth sequence is seed, sprout, sapling, then plant: A–C–B–D.

63.q: Four sentences are given: A. When it saw me, it moved quickly and hid itself in a coconut shell. B. I quietly went near and closed the mouth of the coconut shell with a stone. C. One day I saw a small snake in the compound. D. It was crawling along slowly. Select the correct order.
63.explanation: The event proceeds from seeing the snake (C), to its slow movement (D), its hiding (A), and closing the shell (B).

64.q: Four sentences describe buying a product online: A. Add the product to your shopping cart. B. Select the brand you like. C. Enter the card details and buy the product online. D. Look for the product you want to purchase. Select the correct order.
64.explanation: First find the product (D), select its brand (B), add it to the cart (A), then enter payment details (C).

65.explanation: Traffic increases (C), the road runs out of space (D), the man rides on the pavement (A), and a car hits him when he tries to re-enter the road (B).

81.q: The doctor with his interns are due to arrive here by noon. Identify the segment containing the grammatical error.
81.explanation: The head subject is the singular “doctor”; the verb should be “is due,” so the error is in “interns are due.”

82.explanation: For possession, use “Do you have your own transport?” rather than “Are you having.”

86.explanation: “Lali” is singular, so the present-perfect auxiliary is “has.”

87.explanation: “Was mending” is the grammatical past-continuous form for the action described.

88.explanation: The modal “will” forms the future passive: “will not be eaten.”

89.q: Zira __________ his future wife at the park.
89.explanation: The simple past “met” is the grammatical form for the completed event described.

90.q: The ants __________ working hard all winter.

91.q: The police __________ having convicted the man.

92.q: The kind woman __________ the little infant as her own.

aao-2024-arithmetic.evidence: Questions 1–100 have been checked against the printed pages (pages 1–10) and the final answer key. Stems, four options and calculations were verified. Q75 is held out for a key/ratio conflict, Q70 for a missing assumption, Q30 is compensated, and Q37 is editorially completed. Q100’s printed “board” is corrected to “broad” for readability.

1.q: The value of √2 up to three places of decimal is—
1.explanation: √2 ≈ 1.414213…, which rounds to 1.414 to three decimal places.

2.q: The smallest perfect square number which is divisible by 15, 24 and 25 is—
2.explanation: The least common multiple is 600. Its prime factorization is 2³·3·5²; to make all exponents even, multiply by 2·3=6, giving 3600.

3.q: The number 675 is to be multiplied by which smallest number so that the resulting number will become a perfect cube?
3.explanation: 675 = 3³·5². Multiplying by 5 makes the exponents multiples of three: 675×5 = 3³·5³ = 15³.

6.q: The HCF of two numbers is 16 and their LCM is 160. If one number is 32, then the other number is—
6.explanation: For two integers, their product is HCF×LCM. The other number is (16×160)/32 = 80.

7.q: The number of terms in the sequence 4, 11, 18, …, 186 is—
7.explanation: This is an arithmetic progression with first term 4 and common difference 7. Solve 4+(n−1)7=186 to get n=27.

8.q: The 8th term of the arithmetic progression 9, 6, 3, 0, … is—
8.explanation: The first term is 9 and the common difference is −3. The eighth term is 9+7(−3)=−12.

9.q: Rama gets 49% marks in an examination, obtaining 294 marks. The percentage of marks obtained by his friend in the same examination, who scores 372 marks, is—
9.explanation: 294 is 49% of 600, so the maximum is 600. The friend’s percentage is 372/600×100 = 62%.

10.q: If the length of a rectangle is increased by 20% and the breadth is decreased by 20%, then the area decreases by—
10.explanation: The new area factor is 1.20×0.80=0.96, so the area decreases by 4%.

11.q: A shopkeeper sells two shirts at ₹1995 each. On one he gains 5% and on the other he loses 5%. His gain or loss in the whole transaction is—
11.explanation: When two items are sold at the same price with equal gain/loss rates, the net result is a loss of 5²/100 = 0.25%.

12.q: What rate percent is one minute 48 seconds to an hour?
12.explanation: One minute 48 seconds is 108 seconds. As a share of an hour: 108/3600×100 = 3%.

13.q: Three numbers are in the ratio 2:3:5. If the sum of their squares is 1862, then the first number is—
13.explanation: Let the numbers be 2k, 3k and 5k. Then 38k²=1862, so k=7 and the first number is 14.

14.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 2:3 and if 8 is added to each of them, they become in the ratio 3:4. The numbers are—
14.explanation: Let them be 2x and 3x. Solving (2x+8)/(3x+8)=3/4 gives x=8, so the numbers are 16 and 24.

15.q: The average height of 30 students out of a class of 40 is 160 cm and that of the remaining students is 156 cm. The average height of the whole class is—
15.explanation: The total height is 30×160 + 10×156 = 6360 cm. Divide by 40 to get 159 cm.

16.q: The mean of ten numbers is 40. If the mean of the first five is 42 and that of the last four is 35, the 6th number is—
16.explanation: The ten-number total is 400. The first five sum to 210 and the last four to 140; subtracting these nine numbers leaves the sixth as 50.

17.q: The mean weight of 5 men is increased by 1 kg when one of them, whose weight is 60 kg, is replaced by a new man. The weight of the new man is—
17.explanation: Increasing the mean by 1 kg raises the total by 5 kg. The replacement therefore weighs 60+5=65 kg.

18.q: Two pipes fill a tank in 10 hours and 12 hours respectively, while a third pipe empties the full tank in 20 hours. If all three pipes operate simultaneously, in how much time will the tank be filled?
18.explanation: The net rate is 1/10+1/12−1/20 = 2/15 tank per hour, so filling takes 15/2 = 7.5 hours.

19.q: If 8 men can reap 80 hectares in 24 days, how many hectares can 36 men reap in 30 days?
19.explanation: Output is proportional to workers and days: 80×(36×30)/(8×24)=450 hectares.

20.q: The speed of a moving car is 36 km/hr. This speed in m/sec is—
20.explanation: Convert km/h to m/s by multiplying by 5/18: 36×5/18=10 m/s.

21.q: Two persons start from the same place and walk in opposite directions at 5 km/hr and 4 km/hr respectively. At the end of 3 hours, the distance between them is—
21.explanation: Their separation speed is 5+4=9 km/hr. In 3 hours they are 9×3=27 km apart.

22.q: “A” and “B” are 30 km apart and walk towards each other. “A” is walking at the rate of 4 km/hr and “B” at 6 km/hr. They will meet after—
22.explanation: Their combined closing speed is 4+6=10 km/hr. The meeting time is 30/10=3 hours.

23.q: While walking at 3/5 of the usual speed, a man reaches his destination 10 minutes late. What is his usual time to reach his destination?
23.explanation: At 3/5 speed, travel time becomes 5/3 of normal. The extra 2/3 of the normal time is 10 minutes, so the usual time is 15 minutes.

24.q: Liana’s age is 16 years and his elder sister’s age is 21 years. After how many years will the sum of their ages be 51 years?
24.explanation: Their current ages sum to 37. The total increases by 2 each year, so (51−37)/2=7 years.

25.q: On a plane ground, a man walks 18 m due south, then he turns to his left and walks 6 m due east. He again turns to his left and walks 10 m due north. How far is he now from the starting point?
25.explanation: He is 8 m south and 6 m east of the start. His distance is √(8²+6²)=10 m.

26.q: A sum of money becomes ₹2420 in 2 years and ₹2662 in 3 years. If interest is compounded annually, the rate of interest is—
26.explanation: The ratio of year-3 to year-2 amounts is 2662/2420=1.10, so the annual compound rate is 10%.

27.q: If the perimeter of a circle is numerically equal to the perimeter of a square, then the areas are in the ratio (take π = 22/7)—
27.explanation: Equal perimeters give square side s=πr/2. Thus circle:square area = πr²:s² = 4:π = 14:11 when π=22/7.

28.q: The length of the longest pole that can be kept in a room of dimensions (12 m × 9 m × 8 m) is—
28.explanation: The longest pole is the room’s space diagonal: √(12²+9²+8²)=√289=17 m.

29.q: The volume of a cubical solid is 2744 cm³. Its surface area is—
29.explanation: The cube side is ∛2744=14 cm. Its surface area is 6×14²=1176 cm².

30.q: How many bricks, each measuring (25 cm × 11.25 cm × 6 cm), will be required to construct a wall of dimensions (8 cm × 6 cm × 22.5 cm) if 1/10 of the volume of the wall is occupied by cement mortar?
30.explanation: The official key compensates this item. As printed, the wall dimensions are smaller than a single brick, so none of the listed counts is physically consistent. If the first two wall dimensions were intended to be metres, the calculation would give 5760, but that correction is not supported by the scan; this item is left unscored.
30.reviewNote: The MPSC final key compensates this item; the wall dimensions are smaller than one brick as printed, so it is held out from scoring.

31.q: A kite is flying at a certain height from the horizontal ground. The thread, 100 m long, attached to the kite is tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the thread with the ground is 30°. How high from the ground is the kite flying?
31.explanation: The thread is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. Height=100×sin(30°)=50 m.

32.q: In tossing two coins, the probability of getting two heads is—
32.explanation: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT; only HH has two heads, so the probability is 1/4.

33.q: A bag contains 4 white and some red balls. If the probability of drawing a red ball at random is double that of drawing a white ball, the number of red balls in the bag is—
33.explanation: Let r be the number of red balls. r/(r+4)=2·4/(r+4), so r=8.

34.q: In a committee, 32 people speak Hindi, 14 speak English and 8 speak both Hindi and English. How many speak at least one of the two languages?
34.explanation: By inclusion–exclusion, 32+14−8=38 people speak at least one language.

35.q: In a survey of 200 students in a school, it was found that 125 like orange, 90 like apple and 60 like both orange and apple. How many like neither orange nor apple?
35.explanation: The number who like at least one is 125+90−60=155. Therefore 200−155=45 like neither.

36.q: The cost of a mobile handset is ₹20,000. A lady purchased it by paying ₹12,000 and the balance is to be cleared in two equal instalments of ₹4,500 each. What is the total interest charged under the instalment scheme?
36.explanation: The instalments total ₹9,000 against a financed balance of ₹8,000, so the interest is ₹1,000.

37.q: If (x − 2) is a factor of x³ − 2ax² + ax − 1, then the value [of a] is—
37.explanation: The printed line omits the variable after “value”; the polynomial/options indicate the requested value is a. By the factor theorem, f(2)=8−8a+2a−1=7−6a=0, so a=7/6.

3.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions below.

The ‘Little Tramp’, the unforgettable character Charlie Chaplin invented, was born purely by accident in 1915. While rushing to a film shoot in California, he grabbed clothes other people had left behind in the changing room and, when he emerged, he found he had created a personality everybody loved: a little guy in a bowler hat, a close-fitting jacket, a cane, out-sized shoes and a brush-like moustache.

Before long, Chaplin found himself a star. That puzzled him, for he saw himself essentially as a shy British Music Hall comedian. The U.S. acknowledged him as its king of silent film comedy. Soon, so did crowds all over the world. But life wasn’t always a laugh for Charles Spencer Chaplin. Both his parents were Music Hall artists, who separated when Charlie was very young. His childhood was very sad, for his mother never earned enough to look after Charlie and his older brother, Sydney. Sometimes, Chaplin had to sleep on the streets and forage for food in the garbage.

Charlie took his first bow on stage when his mother made her last appearance. It happened when her voice broke during a song. Her son stepped on stage and sang a popular song. That’s when a star was born. Through all these years of success, Charlie never forgot his troubled childhood. It made him recall a Christmas when he was denied two oranges and his bag of sweets for breaking a rule at the orphanage he went to after his mother’s death. It would have broken his heart if the other children had not offered him a share of theirs. Spontaneously, the adult Chaplin gifted the orphanage with a motion picture machine and insisted that each child should have as many oranges and sweets as they pleased.

(a) Which unforgettable character did Charlie Chaplin invent? (2)
(b) Describe the personality created by Charlie, whom everybody loved. (2)
(c) What did Charlie see himself as? (2)
(d) Give two reasons to show that Charlie Chaplin’s early life was very sad. (2)
(e) When did Charlie Chaplin start his career? (2)
(f) Choose the word in the passage that means ‘to search for food’: (i) stepped (ii) forage (iii) emerged (iv) orphanage. (1)
(g) Choose the meaning of ‘invented’: (i) created (ii) wrote (iii) struggled (iv) laughed. (1)
(h) Find the word in the passage opposite in meaning to ‘bold’: (i) found (ii) shy (iii) silent (iv) puzzled. (1)
(i) Find the word in the passage opposite in meaning to ‘failure’: (i) troubled (ii) share (iii) motion (iv) success. (1)
(j) Find the word in the passage similar in meaning to ‘appeared’: (i) insisted (ii) offered (iii) emerged (iv) broken. (1)
3.explanation: Answer guide: (a) the Little Tramp; (b) a little man wearing a bowler hat, close-fitting jacket, carrying a cane, with oversized shoes and a brush-like moustache; (c) a shy British Music Hall comedian; (d) his parents separated, the family was poor, and he sometimes slept on the streets and searched rubbish for food; (e) when his mother’s voice broke during a song and he stepped on stage to sing. Objective choices: (f) forage (ii), (g) created (i), (h) shy (ii), (i) success (iv), (j) emerged (iii). The source prints two marks for (a)–(e) and one for (f)–(j).

Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it:

Studies serve for delight, for ornament, and for ability. Their chief use for delight is in privateness and retiring; for ornament is in this course; and for ability is in the judgment and disposition of business. For expert men can execute, and perhaps judge of particulars, one by one; but the general counsels, and the plots and marshalling of affairs, come best, from those that are learned. To spend too much time in studies is sloth; to use them too much for ornaments is affectation; to make judgement wholly by their rules, is the humour of a scholar. They perfect nature, and are perfected by experience: for natural abilities are like natural plants that need pruning, by study; and studies themselves do give forth directions too much at large, except they be bounded in by experience. Crafty men condemn studies, simple men admire them, and wise men use them; for they teach not their own use; but that is a wisdom without them, and above them, won by observation. Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse but to weigh and consider.

(d) Which kind of human beings denounce studies? (2 marks)
(e) According to the author, why should one read? (2 marks)
4.explanation: Suggested answers: (a) Studies serve for delight, ornament and ability. (d) Crafty men condemn studies. (e) Read to weigh and consider, not merely to contradict, accept without question, or make conversation.
